item.title: DOJ tells court lawful self-defense carry is allowed in public national park buildings (Zimmerman v. Blanche)
item.description:
STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW

What's new: In an Oct. 2, 2026 motion to dismiss in Zimmerman v. Blanche (N.D. Tex., Fort Worth, No. 4:26-cv-00372-Y, ECF 22), the Justice Department told the court that 18 U.S.C. § 930(a) does not prohibit a person who may lawfully carry from carrying a handgun for self-defense in national park facilities that are open to the public, such as visitor centers or shops. DOJ relies on the August 2026 Office of Legal Counsel opinion that read § 930(d)(3)'s "lawful purposes" exception to cover self-defense carry in publicly accessible post offices, says that opinion binds the Executive Branch, and calls its application to the plaintiffs' conduct "self-evident." On that basis DOJ argues the plaintiffs (Gary Zimmerman, Lisa Ventura, FPC and SAF) face no credible threat of prosecution and lack standing. It also argues there are no firearms restrictions under 36 C.F.R. § 1.5 in the 15 parks Zimmerman plans to visit. The filing was first reported today by AmmoLand (Oct. 6, ~10:34 AM ET).

Why it matters: This is DOJ's position in a federal court filing, extending the OLC post-office reading to public National Park Service buildings. It is not a court ruling or an injunction, and it does not repeal § 930. AmmoLand notes that, as of Oct. 6, the National Park Service's firearms page still describes a prohibition in facilities such as visitor centers and ranger stations. Courthouses, secured areas and nonpublic areas remain outside DOJ's reading. The court has not ruled on the motion.

Verification: VERIFIED from the filed DOJ memorandum (ECF 22, filed 10/02/26). The AmmoLand characterization of the NPS webpage was not independently checked.

item.title: Written opinion explains denial of injunction against Maryland Glock ban (Bathras v. Moore)
item.description:
STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW

Maryland Glock ban: Judge Bennett's written reasoning in Bathras v. Moore is out (preliminary injunction still denied)

What's new: Bearing Arms (Cam Edwards, posted Tue Oct 6 about 10:29 AM ET) quotes U.S. District Judge Richard D. Bennett's written decision explaining his Sep 25 bench denial of a preliminary injunction against Maryland SB 334 in Bathras v. Moore (D. Md. No. 1:26-cv-02074-RDB, consolidated with Duffy v. Moore, No. 1:26-cv-02647-RDB). As quoted, Bennett assumed the law implicates the Second Amendment's plain text, then held Maryland carried its historical burden because SB 334 is "consistent with restrictions on excessively dangerous weapons which have been regulated in response to their criminal misuse and lethality." He called the law "a commensurate response" to technological advances and "today's unrelenting tide of mass shootings and gun violence," applied the Fourth Circuit's "nuanced approach" from the Maryland assault-weapons case (Bianchi), and, per the report, accepted essentially all of the state's analogues (gunpowder storage laws, Bowie knife restrictions, 20th-century short-barreled firearm rules).

Why it matters: This is the first written explanation of the ruling, and it is the order plaintiffs (SAF, FPC, NRA, Atlantic Guns, Maryland Shall Issue and others) would take to the Fourth Circuit. It reaches the opposite result from the Sep 30 D. Conn. preliminary injunction against Connecticut's similar "convertible pistol" law (Glock v. Griffin), so two district courts now disagree on these bans. SB 334 bars manufacture, sale, purchase, receipt and transfer of covered pistols starting Jan 1, 2027; pistols already owned are grandfathered. Both rulings are preliminary, not final merits judgments.

Verified vs. unverified: Verified: Bearing Arms published direct quotes from the written decision today. Not independently verified: the docket entry number and exact filing date of the written opinion (public docket mirrors were unreachable this hour). No notice of appeal found yet.

Also checked, no change: SCOTUS dockets for Duncan v. Bonta 25-198, Gator's 25-153 and NAGR 25-421 show no new entries and no grant; a CNNBC page claiming the Court "agreed to hear" an assault-weapons challenge is not supported by the dockets. Novotny v. Moore 25-1324 remains distributed for the Oct 9 conference. ATF's post-Silencer Shop NFA guidance is still not published.

item.title: San Diego County sues filament maker Polymaker over ghost-gun marketing
item.description: STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW San Diego County sues 3D-printer filament maker Polymaker over ghost-gun marketing WHAT'S NEW: On Oct 5, 2026, San Diego County Counsel Damon Brown filed People v. Polymaker LLC in San Diego Superior Court. It's the County, not the City. GIFFORDS Law Center and White & Case are co-counsel. It was one of the first three suits from the County's new Consumer Fairness and Public Protection unit; the other two target AppLovin and Roblox. The case number was blank on the posted copy and is unverified. THE CLAIM: A single count under California's Unfair Competition Law (Bus. & Prof. Code 17200). The County's theory is that marketing filament for gun-making makes it a regulated "firearm precursor part" under Penal Code 16531. It alleges violations of the precursor-part sales laws, AB 1263's ban on knowingly facilitating illegal gun-making (Civ. Code 3273.625 / Penal Code 29186, effective Jan 1, 2026), and the Firearm Industry Responsibility Act. KEY ALLEGATIONS (none proven): - A "3D Print General PLA Pro" spool sold with YouTuber Sean Aranda's likeness and the slogan "Come and Make It." - Polymaker allegedly sponsored Aranda after YouTube demonetized him, then hired him in Dec 2023. He's now Head of Customer Experience and is not a defendant. - On r/fosscad, asked "Which is better for building guns?", Polymaker's account allegedly recommended PolyLite PLA Pro. - Polymaker's wiki allegedly calls J-B Weld "[p]opular in functional applications like 3D-printed firearms." - In May 2026, SDPD found Polymaker filament, four printed handgun frames and conversion devices at the home of an arrested 16-year-old. The complaint does not allege the marketing caused that purchase. WHAT THE COUNTY WANTS: Civil penalties up to $2,500 per violation (each day counted separately; no total stated), disgorgement of revenue tied to the marketing, injunctions, and attorney's fees. The complaint says it "does not seek to ban the sale of filament in California." POLYMAKER RESPONSE: None found as of about 9 PM ET Oct 5. WHY IT MATTERS: Earlier California cases went after gun-specific products: the Coast Runner mill (same County and GIFFORDS team) and the Gatalog files. This one targets a raw-material maker. Filed 9 days after AB 2047 was signed; the complaint doesn't rely on AB 2047, which covers printers, not filament. Likely fights: whether PLCAA applies to a company without a federal license, vagueness of the "marketing makes it a precursor part" theory, First Amendment (much of the conduct alleged is speech), and possible removal to federal court. SOURCES: - Complaint PDF (County-posted): https://drive.google.com/file/d/11Lf-huSzkf3Z5UGNoFJP2JHG_ex4kcxU/view - County News Center: https://www.countynewscenter.com/county-introduces-new-consumer-fairness-and-public-protection-division-launches-three-major-lawsuits/ - Supervisor Lawson-Remer release: https://www.supervisorterralawsonremer.com/content/d3/us/en/newsroom/newsroom.1791236169387.html - Patch / City News Service: https://patch.com/california/san-diego/new-county-consumer-protection-unit-announces-first-set-lawsuits - GIFFORDS on Coast Runner: https://giffords.org/lawcenter/lawsuit/california-v-coast-runner-holding-ghost-gun-companies-accountable/

item.title: DOJ tells Fifth Circuit under-21 handgun case is moot, pledges no enforcement anywhere
item.description:
DOJ tells Fifth Circuit the under-21 handgun case is moot because it won't enforce the ban against anyone, anywhere (filed Mon Oct 5, 2026).

What's new: In FPC v. ATF (formerly Reese v. ATF; 5th Cir. No. 26-30154; W.D. La. No. 6:20-cv-01438), DOJ filed its brief on today's deadline arguing the appeal over the scope of the injunction is moot. DOJ cites the recent Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinion concluding the federal ban on licensed-dealer handgun sales to 18–20-year-olds is unconstitutional, and says DOJ "will not enforce the challenged provisions against anyone, anywhere." It argues in the alternative that, if the case isn't moot, the OLC opinion gives no basis to expand the injunction, and that ordinary Article III and equitable limits apply to associational plaintiffs.

Why it matters: The district court's injunction covers only FPC and Louisiana Shooting Association members who were members when the suit was filed and who live in the Fifth Circuit. FPC is asking the Fifth Circuit to extend relief to all current and future members, including outside the circuit. DOJ's non-enforcement pledge is a policy position that a future administration could reverse, while a broader injunction would be binding. So the fight is now over how far court-ordered relief reaches, not over whether the ban is constitutional (the Fifth Circuit already held it isn't).

Verification: The filing is reported and quoted by Bearing Arms (Cam Edwards, 3:31 PM ET). The primary brief has not been located publicly yet, so treat the quotes as reported, not independently verified.

Background (already reported): The OLC opinion holding the federal 18–20 handgun ban unenforceable was briefed in mid-September.

item.title: SCOTUS denies Minnesota carry-reciprocity case (Johnson v. Jacobson); Novotny, Duncan magazine petitions still pending
item.description:
STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW

What's new (verified): In its Monday, Oct. 5, 2026 order list (first orders after the Sept. 28 Long Conference), the U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari in Johnson v. Jacobson, No. 26-255, the Liberty Justice Center petition challenging Minnesota's carry-permit reciprocity rules. No justice noted a dissent or wrote a statement on the denial. The Eighth Circuit decision (McCoy and Johnson v. Jacobson, No. 25-3036, judgment May 26, 2026) against the challengers stands.

Questions the petition asked: (1) whether Americans must obtain a firearm license from each state to exercise Second Amendment rights across the nation; (2) whether state reciprocity statutes that don't recognize every other state's license are valid under Bruen. Minnesota waived its response; the Second Amendment Foundation and others filed amicus briefs.

Not acted on (still pending, verified by absence from the order list): Novotny v. Moore, No. 25-1324 (Maryland carry restrictions, rescheduled Sept. 24); Duncan v. Bonta, No. 25-198 (California magazine ban); Gator's Custom Guns, No. 25-153; and NAGR v. Lamont, No. 25-421. No new 2A grants. Viramontes/Grant remain set for argument Dec. 2.

Why it matters: The Court won't take up nationwide carry reciprocity this term through this vehicle, leaving state-by-state permit recognition in place. The bigger magazine and Maryland carry petitions are still alive, likely being relisted or held, so the next order lists matter.

item.title: DOJ formally confirms no appeal of N.D. Tex. NFA ruling (Silencer Shop v. ATF)
item.description:
STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW

DOJ formally confirms it will not appeal the N.D. Tex. NFA ruling (Silencer Shop Foundation v. ATF)

What's new (verified, court filing): In a filing docketed Thu Oct 1, 2026 (ECF 145, Silencer Shop Foundation v. ATF, N.D. Tex. No. 6:25-cv-56-H), DOJ attached a Sept. 24, 2026 letter from Solicitor General D. John Sauer to Congress under 28 U.S.C. § 530D stating "that the Department of Justice has determined not to file an appeal in this case." The letter gives no reasoning. This is the formal follow-through on the CBS report of Sept. 17 that President Trump directed DOJ not to appeal (briefed Sept. 18). Until now that was only a report of intent; it's now on the docket.

Also in the same filing: DOJ says ATF "is currently working to finalize public guidance regarding the NFA." DOJ asked for a 10-day extension (from Oct. 2) to respond to a motion by nine state plaintiffs asking Judge Hendrix to clarify (1) whether the injunction applies statewide to all relevant transfers in those states and (2) whether ATF must notify or identify covered people. The states oppose the extension. No ruling on the extension was found in this check.

Why it matters: The Aug. 5, 2026 final judgment (ECF 136–137) permanently bars enforcement of NFA registration/approval requirements for short-barreled rifles and shotguns, suppressors, and "any other weapons" as to the plaintiffs, their members, and their customers. It is party-limited, not nationwide, and machine guns aren't affected. The government's 60-day appeal window closes Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. The rules still let the court extend that deadline for excusable neglect or good cause, but DOJ has now said in writing that it won't appeal. Still open: the scope question the states raised and ATF's promised guidance.

Timing note: The filing has been public since Oct. 1 and AmmoLand reported it. The watch didn't flag it earlier, so it's being briefed now, ahead of the Oct. 5 deadline.

Sources:
DOJ motion to extend briefing deadline, ECF 145 (filed Oct. 1, 2026)
AmmoLand: DOJ confirms it won't appeal NFA ruling
The Reload (Oct. 4): Is the NFA injunction permanent now?

item.title: NJ asks SCOTUS to hold AWB/mag ban case pending Viramontes
item.description:
What is new: New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport filed a petition for a writ of certiorari dated Oct. 1, 2026 in Davenport v. Association of New Jersey Rifle and Pistol Clubs (with related Cheeseman plaintiffs), seeking Supreme Court review of the Third Circuit’s July 17, 2026 en banc judgment (Nos. 24-2415, 24-2450, 24-250) that invalidated New Jersey’s semi-automatic “assault firearm” and large-capacity magazine restrictions.

Why it matters: The state asks the Court to hold both questions presented pending Viramontes v. Cook County (No. 25-238) and Grant v. Higgins (No. 25-566) (set for argument Dec. 2, 2026), then, if appropriate, grant, vacate, and remand in light of that decision—the same hold/GVR path used for other AWB/LCM petitions. The Third Circuit stayed its mandate on Aug. 4, 2026 pending cert (deadline had been Oct. 15), so New Jersey’s bans remain enforceable under that stay until further order.

Verified: Oct. 1, 2026 petition PDF (face caption “No. 26-___”). Unverified / pending: public SCOTUS docket number—not yet located among Oct. 1–2, 2026 docket entries on supremecourt.gov as of this alert.

item.title: Judge grants preliminary injunction against Connecticut HB 5043 convertible-pistol ban (Glock, NSSF)
item.description:
STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW
Federal judge grants preliminary injunctions to Glock and NSSF against Connecticut's HB 5043 "convertible pistol" ban, one day before its Oct 1, 2026 effective date.

WHAT'S NEW
On Sept. 30, 2026, U.S. District Judge Kari A. Dooley (D. Conn.) filed an "ORDER GRANTING PLAINTIFFS' EMERGENCY MOTION FOR PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION" in two companion cases that were heard together: Glock, Inc. v. Griffin et al., No. 3:26-cv-01525 (KAD), and National Shooting Sports Foundation Inc. et al. v. Griffin et al., No. 3:26-cv-01528 (KAD). It is ECF No. 31 on the Glock docket and resolves Glock's motion (ECF No. 3) and the NSSF plaintiffs' motion (No. 26-cv-1528, ECF No. 4). Conclusion: "Plaintiffs’ Motions for Preliminary Injunctive Relief are GRANTED. A separate Order shall enter."

WHY IT MATTERS
HB 5043 (Public Act 26-41) became law May 26, 2026 and takes effect Oct. 1, 2026. Among other things, it makes it a class D felony for anyone who "distributes, transports or imports into the state, keeps for sale, or offers or exposes for sale, any convertible pistol". The law defines a convertible pistol as a semiautomatic pistol with a cruciform trigger bar that can be readily converted into a machine gun by attaching a pistol converter; hammer-fired pistols are excluded. The court found the plaintiffs likely to win their Second Amendment challenge and likely to suffer irreparable harm, so it granted preliminary relief the day before the ban takes effect.

KEY FACTS
- Parties: Plaintiffs are Glock, Inc. (No. 26-cv-1525) and National Shooting Sports Foundation, Inc., Shadow Systems LLC, and Blue Trail Range Corporation (No. 26-cv-1528). Defendants are Chief State's Attorney Patrick J. Griffin, the State's Attorneys for each judicial district, and (Glock case only) DESPP Commissioner Ronnell A. Higgins, all sued in their official capacities.
- Timeline: Both suits were filed Sept. 21, 2026. The court held a joint hearing Sept. 29, 2026. The order is dated Sept. 30, 2026, signed at Bridgeport.
- Bruen step one conceded: "For purposes of the motion for preliminary injunction only, the Defendants accept that HB 5043 implicates the plain text of the Second Amendment." The court held that this makes the statute "presumptively unconstitutional."
- History argument rejected for now: The state relied on founding-era "proving laws" (PA, NJ, NH, MA) together with the tradition of regulating machine guns. The court held that this reliance, "at this juncture, does not adequately rebut the presumption that the statute is unconstitutional under the Second Amendment." It said proving laws "were not designed to, and indeed could not, forestall future misuse of the firearm (even if predictable) after it enters the stream of commerce." It also found "no dispute that handguns with a cruciform trigger bar (in an unconverted state) are not only safe, but extremely popular for purposes of self-defense".
- Effective-date point: "the Defendants offer no adequate explanation as to how the sale of a firearm manufactured on September 30, 2026 needs no safety regulation but the same firearm manufactured 24 hours later is sufficiently dangerous so as to be properly restricted and regulated by the state."
- Merits holding: "on the present record, the Court concludes that Plaintiffs have met their burden of establishing a likelihood of success on the merits."
- Irreparable harm: The court cited a Blue Trail Range declaration that it holds about $25,000 of cruciform-trigger handguns, expects that inventory to run out by the end of October 2026, and has stopped ordering such handguns because of HB 5043. It also noted the plaintiffs' arguments about losing law-enforcement customers, limits on advertising, and harm to Connecticut citizens' Second Amendment rights. Weighing these together, it concluded: "if not enjoined, enforcement of HB 5043 will cause irreparable harm to Plaintiffs."

CAVEATS
- This is a preliminary injunction, not a final judgment. The court wrote that the result "may derive from the condensed time frame" and that "upon further development of the record, the outcome may well be different."
- The ruling addresses only the Second Amendment claim. Footnote 4: "The Court does not, because it need not, take up the question of whether the Glock SlimLine or Series VI firearms fall outside the scope of the statute." Glock's vagueness and other claims were not decided.
- The operative injunction terms (exact scope and who is bound) are in a "separate Order" that this document says "shall enter." That separate order had not been reviewed when this alert was written.
- The state argued the statute applies only to certain firearms manufactured after Oct. 1, 2026, so existing inventory can still be sold. The court agreed on that point ("That is true, and not in dispute.") but held that it "does not end the inquiry."
- This document does not mention any appeal. The state could seek review in the Second Circuit.
- Page 3 of the order cites the cases as "No. 25-cv-1525" and "No. 25-cv-1528". The caption and header show 3:26-cv-01525 and 3:26-cv-01528, so these appear to be typos in the order.

SOURCES

item.title: 2A alert: 9th Cir. en banc reverses Hawaii gun-permit win (Yukutake v. Lopez) — upholds 30-day buy window + inspection under Bruen n.9
item.description:
2A alert (~1:46 PM ET Tue Sep 22):

Yukutake v. Lopez — Ninth Circuit en banc reverses Hawaii firearm-permit injunction.

What is new:
• U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, en banc, No. 21-16756, opinion filed Sep. 22, 2026.
• Caption: Todd Yukutake; David Kikukawa v. Anne E. Lopez (Hawaii AG); City & County of Honolulu also a defendant. D. Haw. No. 1:19-cv-00578-JMS-RT.
• Opinion by Judge Owens; dissents by Judge R. Nelson (joined in part), Judge Forrest, and Judge VanDyke. Vacates prior three-judge panel affirmance.
• Disposition: REVERSED AND REMANDED.

Holding:
Court holds Hawaii’s shall-issue regime comports with the Second Amendment. Challenged provisions — Haw. Rev. Stat. § 134-2(e) (handgun acquisition permit void unless used within 30 days) and § 134-3 (registration form + bring firearm to police for inspection in certain circumstances) — are treated as presumptively lawful under Bruen footnote 9. Plaintiffs failed to show the provisions were put toward “abusive ends” that would effectively deny ordinary citizens their Second Amendment rights; at most “modest, procedural burdens.”

Why it matters:
En banc reversal after a district-court permanent injunction and a prior panel affirmance for the plaintiffs. Entrenches Bruen n.9 as a practical safe harbor for objective shall-issue conditions in the Ninth Circuit. Dissents argue the majority misreads footnote 9 and that the government still must prove history and tradition.

Caveats:
• Not a ruling on may-issue; majority notes lengthy waits, high fees, etc. could still trigger Second Amendment scrutiny.
• Disposition is reverse and remand; no stay language in the ordered line.
• Forrest dissent also addresses statewide injunction breadth.

Primary source:
https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2026/09/22/21-16756.pdf

item.title: 2A alert: 5th Cir. strikes federal interstate handgun purchase ban (Elite Precision Customs v. ATF, 2–1, Sep 18)
item.description:
2A alert (~5:27 PM ET Fri Sep 18):

Elite Precision Customs v. ATF — Fifth Circuit strikes federal interstate handgun purchase ban.

What is new:
• U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit (No. 25-11206), opinion filed Sep. 18, 2026 (Doc. 83-1).
• Caption: Elite Precision Customs L.L.C.; Tim Herron; Freddie Blish; Firearms Policy Coalition, Inc. v. ATF; AG Todd Blanche; Acting ATF Director Daniel Driscoll.
• Panel: Judge Jerry Smith (author), Judge Engelhardt; Judge Haynes dissenting.
• Holding: the federal “Nonresident Handgun Purchase Ban” — 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(a)(3), 922(a)(5), and 922(b)(3) — is unconstitutional under the Second Amendment.
• Disposition: judgment of dismissal REVERSED; judgment RENDERED for the plaintiffs (appeal from N.D. Tex. No. 4:25-CV-44).

Why it matters:
Those provisions (together) bar direct interstate handgun sales (FFL to out-of-state buyer), with long-gun on-site interstate sales having statutory carve-outs. The court applied Bruen/Rahimi, cited Reese on purchase rights, rejected the Second Circuit’s Vereen approach (Ban upheld; cert denied), and found founding-era analogues inadequate.

Caveats:
• Binding in the Fifth Circuit — not a Supreme Court ruling and not automatically nationwide.
• 2–1 decision; government can seek rehearing en banc or certiorari (opinion silent on stay/mandate timing).
• Final ordered line does not quote “permanent injunction granted” or a nationwide ATF non-enforcement order.
• Court did not independently strike ATF’s parallel regulation 27 C.F.R. § 478.99(a); does not rewrite long-gun interstate rules or decide other § 922 provisions (e.g., age bans).
• SAF is not a party.

Sources:
• Opinion PDF: https://assets.nationbuilder.com/firearmspolicycoalition/pages/10076/attachments/original/1789762991/2026.09.18_083-1_OPINION.pdf?1789762991

item.title: 2A alert: OLC says federal 18–20 handgun purchase ban (922(b)(1)/(c)(1)) unconstitutional as applied — dealers may not face criminal penalties
item.description:
2A alert — DOJ Office of Legal Counsel opinion (Sep 17, 2026):

Title: Application of 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) to Young Adults — Memorandum Opinion for the Attorney General.

What it says:
• OLC concludes §§ 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) are unconstitutional as applied to law-abiding young adults ages 18–20 who seek to purchase handguns from federally licensed dealers.
• Those adults are among “the people”; handguns are arms in common use; barring FFL handgun sales burdens the right to keep and bear arms under Bruen / Wolford.
• Government cannot show a Founding-era tradition that justifies the ban.
• Dealers may not be subjected to criminal penalties for selling handguns to that class.

Caveats (important):
• This is an OLC opinion advising DOJ on enforcement — not a court judgment striking the statute nationwide.
• Scope is handguns / FFL sales. Federal law already allows 18–20 purchases of rifles and shotguns from dealers.
• Does not by itself erase state 21+ handgun laws.

Why it matters:
DOJ’s own Office of Legal Counsel told the Attorney General the Gun Control Act’s 21-for-handguns rule fails Bruen/Wolford for 18–20-year-olds — a major enforcement-side development in the under-21 litigation lane (Reese / McCoy / NRA v. Bondi).
